newsitem.title: GERMANY: Anti-nuclear protesters clash with German police.
newsitem.headline: Anti-nuclear protesters clash with German police.

text.p: Anti-nuclear activists clashed with police on Monday in northern Germany where a train carring a controversial shipment of nuclear waste was due to make a stop on its way to a dump.

Police deployed in Germany's biggest post-war security operation said up to 2,000 activists had defied the authorities ban on demonstrations along the route of the train and were camped around the northern town of Dannenberg.

Environmental groups opposed to the shipment estimated some 10,000 demonstrators were there waiting for the train, carrying six containers of nuclear waste, to arrive on its way to Gorleben medium-term storage depot, east of Hanover.
Some activists blocked one of the roads along the route the controversial cargo was expected to take with burning barricades as a protest ahead of the shipment's arrival.
Others tried to damage roads by tunnelling under them. Police said it was possible one road would have to be closed.

Militant protesters pelted riot police with stones. Other demonstrators played cat-and-mouse with police and border troops by disappearing when they arrived and then resurfacing to continue their obstruction.
The train set off from the southern town of Walheim early on Monday and made its way northwards across Germany.
Some 30,000 police and border troops lined tracks along its route wearing riot helmets and carrying batons while police helicopters circled overhead.
The security operation will cost at least 66 million marks ($39 million) and surpass the 46 million marks spent on bringing a smaller shipment to Gorleben last year.
The containers were to be loaded on Tuesday on to flat-bed trailers in Dannenberg, each drawn by a truck.
These were then to be taken by road to Gorleben, some 20 km (14 miles) away, where thousands more activists were already camped and awaiting its arrival, probably on Wednesday.

Police said in general the protests were peaceful but local government officials condemned them. "Digging under roads has nothing to do with peaceful opposition," said Ulrike Wolff-Gebhardt, head of a town council in the Dannenberg area.
Greens leader Gunda Roestel told Saar radio her party valued the protests as "a symbol against atomic energy policy" and called for peaceful resistance.
"There is only one alternative for the (government's energy) concept -- to abolish atomic power in the face of popular protest," Roestel said.
Opposition Social Democrats (SPD) criticised the government's energy policy, saying the people were against it because they realised it posed risks to health and environment.

Transporting nuclear waste around the country was not necessary, "but rather it is the consequence of a false, dubious and failed concept of re-processing of nuclear waste," said SPD environment spokesman in parliament, Michael Mueller.
Earlier, police removed anti-nuclear activists who staged a sit-down protest on rail tracks near the northern city of Goettingen, delaying the nuclear waste train for 20 minutes.
